title: Older People and Palliative Care
full_title: Medicine for Older People and Palliative Care
tagline: Ageing and frailty, falls, delirium, polypharmacy, symptom control and care at the end of life
summary: An ageing population makes the care of older people central to medicine. This course covers ageing and frailty, comprehensive geriatric assessment, falls, delirium and dementia care, polypharmacy and deprescribing, and palliative care: symptom control, communication and care at the end of life.
overview: Older patients are not young patients with more diseases: physiology loses reserve, presentations flatten to 'confusion' or a fall, several conditions and a dozen drugs interact, and the ward environment itself becomes a hazard. Geriatric medicine is the specialty of the multifactorial problem — the same symptoms arising from many causes at once — and its methods are comprehensive assessment, an interdisciplinary team, and honesty about goals. This course teaches the core syndromes: frailty and ageing, falls, delirium and dementia care, and polypharmacy.

Palliative medicine is presented as the other half of the same skill: relieving suffering when cure is no longer on the table, which is a positive treatment for its own sake and applies early in disease, not only in the last days. Chapters cover palliative care principles and prognostication, symptom control — pain and the WHO ladder logic, breathlessness, nausea, delirium, fatigue — and end-of-life care: the dying patient, anticipatory prescribing, the last hours, bereavement, and the legal and ethical framework around advance planning and decisions to limit treatment.

The approach is practical and quantitative where possible: the assessment tools (AMT, 4AT, FRAX, Rockwood scale), falls-risk factors and multifactorial intervention, delirium screening, the deprescribing process, opioid conversion arithmetic and laxative prophylaxis, and the epidemiology of ageing that makes this the largest growing patient group in every hospital. All cases are fictional and all management statements describe principles under current guidance.
outcomes: Describe the physiology of ageing and its clinical consequences (reduced reserve, altered pharmacokinetics, atypical presentation), and use frailty concepts and assessment tools to stratify risk and plan care.
Carry out a comprehensive geriatric assessment across physical, cognitive, psychological and social domains, and formulate a multifactorial problem list and management plan.

Assess an older person after a fall — intrinsic, extrinsic and drug causes, syncope versus mechanical fall — and outline multifactorial prevention including strength and balance training and home hazard reduction.
Distinguish delirium from dementia and depression, apply a screening tool, identify and treat precipitants, and describe prevention and non-pharmacological management of delirium on general wards.
Explain the epidemiology and subtypes of dementia, the principles of dementia care including behavioural and psychological symptoms, and caregiver support.
Apply the logic of polypharmacy: identify prescribing cascades and potentially inappropriate medicines, conduct a structured medication review, and deprescribe safely with monitoring.
Define palliative care and its timing, discuss goals-of-care conversations and prognosis, and describe multidisciplinary and advance care planning practice.

Manage the common palliative symptoms — pain (analgesic ladder and opioid arithmetic including conversions and equi-antianalgesic dosing), breathlessness, nausea, secretions, constipation, itching and fatigue — and recognise the recognisable dying phase with its anticipatory symptom plan.

Discuss death, after-death care, bereavement support and the legal essentials (verification, certification, and the distinction between symptom control, sedation and hastening death under relevant law).

history.title: A disease of the cortex described
history.detail: Alois Alzheimer presents the case of Auguste D. — presenile dementia with disorientation, memory failure and, at autopsy, cortical plaques and neurofibrillary tangles — turning 'second childhood' from a descriptive phrase into a pathological entity that would take a century to begin to explain.

history.title: Geriatrics named
history.detail: Ignatz Nascher, a New York physician, coins 'geriatrics' and argues that the ailments of old age form a coherent field requiring its own expertise, at a time when the pauper wards where most elderly people were cared for offered them little of any kind.

history.title: Longitudinal study of ageing
history.detail: Nathan Shock's Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging begins, following healthy volunteers of all ages with repeated physiological measurement — the design that established which functions decline with years and which with disease, and the model for a hundred cohort studies of ageing.

history.title: Measuring what patients can do
history.detail: Sidney Katz's index of activities of daily living, developed with the geriatricians of the Jewish Geriatric Home in Brooklyn, gives the field its first standard outcome — can she dress, walk, eat, toilet, bathe, transfer — and makes functional assessment as routine as blood pressure.

history.title: St Christopher's Hospice
history.detail: Nurse-physician-social worker Cicely Saunders opens St Christopher's Hospice in Sydenham with the then-radical ideas that total pain — physical, psychological, social, spiritual — can be controlled by a dedicated team, that hospice is a place to live, and that dying need not mean dying alone in an unscheduled bed.

history.title: Hospice becomes an entitlement
history.detail: The US Medicare hospice benefit, won after Florence Wald’s Connecticut Hospice (1974) proved the model's viability, makes interdisciplinary palliative care reimbursed rather than charitable; the specialty's growth in North America follows, alongside the hospice movements already spreading from Britain.

history.title: The get-up-and-go test
history.detail: After George Isaacs's work on the post-fall syndrome and his 'get up and go' bedside test, Anne Podsiadlo and Susan Richardson formalise the Timed Up and Go: rise, walk three metres, turn, sit — with a measurable cut-off for fall risk, one of the rare bedside tests that predicts a hard outcome.

history.title: Frailty operationalised
history.detail: Linda Fried and colleagues, using the Women's Health and Aging Studies cohorts, define the frailty phenotype — weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slowness, low activity — and show it predicts falls, institutionalisation and death; geriatric medicine acquires a screenable syndrome rather than a vibes-based description.
